newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait, China in talks on controversial gun deal.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait, China in talks on controversial gun deal.

text.p: Kuwait and China are discussing a $200 million arms deal which has been strongly criticised by the Gulf state's main ally the United States.

Western military and diplomatic sources said on Monday that a Kuwaiti military team had left for China for follow up talks on the proposed purchase of Chinese 155mm tracked howitzer guns for the Kuwait Land Forces.
"We thought the team was to go in August but now we are told it has already left for China," said a Western military source, who closely follows the deal for the self-propelled guns.
An MP has presented the defence ministry with a request for details on the deal and the sending of a team to Beijing after a Kuwaiti military committee recommended buying the Chinese gun.
That deal and another for British naval missiles may be discussed in parliament on Tuesday ahead of a summer recess.

There has been no official announcement on the China guns. But the sources said a Kuwaiti military committee had in May recommended that the Chinese equip one battalion with 18 howitzers with an option for arming a second battalion.

Arab and Western officials told Reuters the decision was largely a political one after China, a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, suggested it might veto the renewal of United Nations sanctions imposed on Iraq since 1990 for its invasion of the Gulf state.
News of the purchase prompted State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns to urge Kuwait to buy American, reminding reporters: "We had a war (in 1991) to liberate Kuwait...
"We saved Kuwait. We saved the royal family. And we saved the economy...And we assume that Kuwait hasn't forgotten that."
Although Kuwait did not respond publicly, Western diplomats said the tiny state and its ruling al-Sabah family were offended by what Burns said.

"The best way to convince a friend is privately, between yourselves," said a Gulf Arab official. "Not publicly like this, nobody can stand it and could result in moving in the other (China) direction."

British and U.S. ministers have in recent weeks privately advised Kuwait against the Chinese option, arguing it was inferior to what they had on offer and also incompatible with the Gulf state's mainly Western weapons.

Washington still hopes Kuwait would buy its M109 A6 Paladin, which is also deployed with U.S. troops in Kuwait. The British are lobbying hard for their Desert AS90 while South Africa offered its LIW 155mm G6, the only wheeled system in the race.
Some diplomats said Burns's remarks were not the official policy but personal views, a point which was made to Kuwait.
